name: Carlos Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Mrs Ashworth at Longmeadow, which is beef cattle and hay. We've got about a hundred and forty suckler cows, that's cows that raise their own calves, and three hundred acres of grass we cut for hay and silage. In winter my day is feeding, bedding the sheds with straw, checking water troughs that freeze, and then whatever's broken. In summer it's all hay, and you live by the weather forecast.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best is calving at night when it goes right, a calf up and drinking within the hour and you're stood there in the shed light feeling like you did something. Worst is that I'm still not good on the baler. Last July I jammed it twice in one afternoon and Mrs Ashworth didn't say a word, which was worse than shouting.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I'll ask a chatbot to explain something on a feed label, or check what a vet's note means before I ring her back. I don't trust it on anything I can't check, though. My partner Lina's a primary teacher and she uses it far more, for lesson plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's handy and that's about it. At the mart I'd tell the older lads it's like having a nephew who's read every manual. Online I'd say nothing, I'm not a poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it changes very little for me. Cows still calve when they calve and hay still needs three dry days. It might make me a bit quicker at the paperwork Mrs Ashworth hands me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it for the movement forms and the medicine records, the dull bits, so I've more time on the baler. I'd book myself on the machinery course at the college in the spring, which I've been putting off. And Lina and I would keep putting money into the house fund like we already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Fine, really, like a normal year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the house fund.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've got just over a year of my wages saved, between us, plus a bit my dad gave us when he sold his garage. We want a place with a bit of land, maybe two acres. Not to farm properly, just for a few calves of our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone on the farm who'd be against even this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dennis, who does the contract hedging and some of the hay, thinks computers are a plot to make farmers fill in more forms. He's not completely wrong. He'd still ask me to look things up on my phone for him.

S0.say: I'd say it's handy, like having a nephew who's read every manual. I'd say that at the cattle market but wouldn't post about it online.
S0.think: I think it changes very little for me, because cows calve when they calve and hay needs three dry days. It might just make the paperwork a bit quicker.
S0.do: Uses AI for movement forms and medicine records to free up time to practise on the baler. Books the spring machinery course at the college and keeps adding to the house fund with Lina.
S0.quote: It's like having a nephew who's read every manual.
S0.fieldNote: Carlos is open about being weak on machinery, and the jammed baler story is clearly still with him. His cushion comes partly from his dad selling a garage, and the couple are saving for a small plot. He uses AI as a checker, not a guide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not fair on young people if companies stop hiring beginners. I was a beginner two years ago, and Mrs Ashworth took a chance on me. I'd say that in the farmers' group chat, and probably get told I'm soft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm just about in, and I'm grateful I got in before the door closed. But I'm still below average at this job, so I'd want to get good quick. If I left Longmeadow, would the next farm take on someone who jams a baler?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put at Longmeadow and get good, that's the plan. I'd ask Mrs Ashworth if I can take over the hay contractor's diary and the fertiliser orders, so I'm useful in more ways. I'd also join the farmworkers' union, because if fewer beginners get taken on, somebody should be making noise about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared. More like a reminder to stop coasting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people in the group chat would call you soft. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a group of young farmers from round here, mostly sons and daughters of owners. They'll say it's just the market. They're all going to inherit a farm, so it's easy for them to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Lina think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's more worried than me, because schools hire beginners too and she's only in her third year. We had a long talk about it one night. We agreed whoever's job looks wobblier gets first call on the savings.

S1.say: I'd say it's not fair on young people if companies stop hiring beginners, since Mrs Ashworth took a chance on me. I'd post that in the young farmers' group chat and expect to be called soft.
S1.think: I think I got in just before the door closed, and I'm grateful for it. But I'm still below average, so I'd need to get good fast in case I ever have to move farms.
S1.do: Stays at Longmeadow and asks to take over the hay contractor's diary and fertiliser orders. Joins the farmworkers' union and agrees with Lina that whoever looks less secure gets first call on their savings.
S1.feel: Uneasy, as a nudge to stop coasting rather than real fear.
S1.quote: They're all going to inherit a farm, so it's easy for them to say.
S1.fieldNote: His left-leaning views come out as a sense of fairness about who gets a first chance, and some edge toward farmers' children who'll inherit. The pact with Lina over the savings is very practical. He wants to widen his role before anything forces it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to look after the people losing office jobs, with proper money while they retrain. And I'd say it shouldn't just be the tech companies who get rich. I'd probably share something from the union about it, which would be a first for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it probably doesn't touch me much. Nobody's going to make an AI that beds a shed. What it touches is the stuff round the edges: the agent who sells our cattle, the people at the feed company, maybe the vet's receptionist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job, keep saving, keep going to the union. I'd try out whatever new AI tools turn up for farm records once a couple of neighbours have used them and they work. And I'd tell Lina's brother, who does insurance claims, to look hard at that course in electrical work he keeps talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious for other people, and a bit lucky, which is an odd mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for neighbours to try a tool first. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen what happens when you buy first. Mrs Ashworth paid for a weighing system for the cattle three years ago and the software company went bust. The scales are still there, we just write the weights on the wall in chalk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who'd you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lina's brother, Tomas. He's twenty-four and he's done nothing but claims since school. He's clever, but he'd be one of thousands looking for the same new job.

S2.say: I'd say the government must give people losing office jobs proper money while they retrain, and that tech companies shouldn't keep all the gains. I'd probably share a union post about it, a first for me.
S2.think: I think it barely touches me, because no AI is going to bed a shed. It hits the jobs around the edges, like the cattle agent, the feed company and the vet's receptionist.
S2.do: Keeps working, saving and going to union meetings. Tries new farm-record tools only after a couple of neighbours prove them, and urges Lina's brother to start the electrical course.
S2.feel: Anxious for others and lucky for himself, which feels like an odd mix.
S2.quote: The scales are still there, we just write the weights on the wall in chalk.
S2.fieldNote: The chalk weights on the shed wall explain his whole approach to new tech: wait until it's proven. He's clear he's mostly safe here, and his worry goes to his partner's brother. He's starting to become a bit more political, though gently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should be shared, through taxes on the big companies and on property, and I'd say it to anyone. If share and house prices boom while people are losing jobs, the government has to step in. I'd go on a march if the union organised one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be torn. The house we want would cost a lot more, so our savings would buy less. But we'd still both have jobs, which is more than a lot of people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Lina and decide whether to buy a small place before prices go even higher, or wait. I think we'd wait, rent, and keep the money safe. At work I'd be ready for people asking about farm jobs, and I'd tell Mrs Ashworth to take on a beginner if she can, because I was one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Annoyed more than scared. Frustrated that the thing we saved for moves away from us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell your boss to hire a beginner. Would she listen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She might. She's tough but fair, and she says the farm needs young people or it dies with her. She's sixty-one and her kids aren't interested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So who do you think gets the gains, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People who already own houses and shares. My dad, a bit, with the money from the garage. Mrs Ashworth, with the land. Not Tomas, not the people in offices who just lost their jobs.

S3.say: I'd say the gains must be shared through taxes on big companies and property, and the government has to step in. I'd join a union march if there was one.
S3.think: Privately I'm torn, because the house we're saving for would cost much more. But we'd both still have jobs, which is more than many people.
S3.do: Talks with Lina about whether to buy before prices rise, and they choose to keep renting and keep the money safe. Encourages Mrs Ashworth to take on a beginner from the people looking for farm work.
S3.feel: Annoyed and frustrated that the house they saved for keeps moving out of reach, more than scared.
S3.quote: The thing we saved for moves away from us.
S3.fieldNote: His savings help him less here, because the boom pushes the house further off. He's quick to list who wins, including his own father, without bitterness. Mrs Ashworth having no successor is worth noting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the robots should be owned or at least taxed so the people they replace get something. And I'd say it's not just factory jobs anymore, it's us now. I'd be at the union meetings every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one shakes me. I'm the least skilled person at Longmeadow, and if a robot can feed, bed and check the troughs, Mrs Ashworth doesn't need me. She'd still need someone for calving, maybe, but that's her, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't jump straight away. I'd watch what the first robot can actually do in our sheds, because the ground's rough and the cattle push everything over. If it works, I'd ask to be the one trained on it, and I'd take that machinery course I keep putting off. And Lina and I would use the savings to buy those two acres while I've still got wages coming in, so we've at least got something of our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly, for the first time in this whole talk. But not helpless, because of the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first day of a robot at Longmeadow look like, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some man from the dealer with a tablet, and Mrs Ashworth with her arms folded. The robot would do the feed passage fine. Then a heifer would knock it over and Dennis would laugh for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see, but also buy land straight away. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I think. I'd wait and see at work, because I don't want to panic and quit a good job. But I'd buy the land fast, because if robots take the hands-on jobs, owning a bit of ground is the only safe thing left.

S4.say: I'd say robots should be owned by or taxed for the people they replace, because now it's farm jobs too, not just factories. I'd be at union meetings every week.
S4.think: This one shakes me, because I'm the least skilled person at Longmeadow. If a robot can feed, bed and check troughs, Mrs Ashworth doesn't need me.
S4.do: Watches how the first robot copes with rough ground and pushy cattle before deciding anything at work. Asks to be trained on it, takes the machinery course and uses savings to buy two acres with Lina while wages still come in.
S4.feel: Scared for the first time in the interview, but not helpless because of the savings.
S4.quote: Then a heifer would knock it over and Dennis would laugh for a week.
S4.fieldNote: Carlos holds two moves at once: wait at work, act fast on land. He resolved the contradiction himself when asked. His humour about the heifer and Dennis softens real fear about being the least skilled person on the farm.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robot one, the last. The others hit people I care about, but that one hits me directly. What would help is training that's paid and close to home, so a farm worker can learn the machines without losing wages, and some rule that a share of what the robots save goes to the people they replaced.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who owns the land. Everyone talks about jobs, but round here the real question is who owns the ground the robots work on. If it's all big companies, the rest of us are just visitors.

headlineQuote: If it's all big companies, the rest of us are just visitors.
portrait: Carlos is a 27-year-old junior on a beef and hay farm, warm and self-mocking about his weak spot with the baler, saving with his teacher partner Lina for two acres of their own. He uses AI now and then as a checker and waits for neighbours to prove new tools first, after watching a cattle-weighing system go dead. His left-leaning politics are about fairness, a first chance for beginners and sharing the gains, and he grows more active through the pictures. He's calm until the robot picture, which scares him, and his answer is to stay steady at work while buying land fast.
biggestWorry: The robot picture, because it hits him directly as the least skilled worker on the farm.
whatWouldHelp: Paid training close to home so farm workers can learn the machines without losing wages, and a rule that a share of what robots save goes to the people they replace.
